https://www.vanguardngr.com/2026/08/i-tr.text: Home » The Arts » I try to be Afrocentric in my writings — Obinna Chilekezi The Arts Follow us on Google August 2, 2026 I try to be Afrocentric in my writings — Obinna Chilekezi By Chris Onuoha Obinna Chilekezi is a poet, author, teacher, literary critic and research fellow including insurance expert. His passion for creative writing, poetry precisely, spans over three decades with lots of publications to his credit. The Imo State-born social commentator, in this interview describes his journey into literary world as one with multifaceted background. Excerpts: How would you describe yourself, believing it will make sense? I don’t know how to start. Simply, I can say that I have multifaceted background, having read library science, publishing and journalism before vying into the business studies through reading banking and finance, market, insurance, and lastly entrepreneurship at the doctorate level. Although I worked very briefly with Daily Times where I started writing in 1985 (had articles in Sunday Times, Business Times and my first poem in Times International); I can say that all my life I have worked and still working in the insurance industry. It is important to note that I started writing before I joined the insurance and I can say that it was like I forgot writing while being active in the insurance sector until few years back that I went back to writing. Could you recount events, things, places or people that inspired your passion into writing particularly poem appreciation? I will say that all of them; that is events, things, places and people had inspired my writing. I will also wish to note the influence of my mother which should be story for another day. Nevertheless, I will prefer to acknowledge two people who had inspired me physically to write poetry. The first was one Dr Onukaogu. I cannot recollect his first name. He was our ‘Use of English’ lecturer at the then College of Technology Owerri (COTECH), who would come to class and be reciting poems to us. I came in to read information science with my secondary school subjects in Physics, Chemistry and Biology and a pass in Mathematics that prevented me from reading sciences. Dr Onukaogu would give copies of poems to read. Initially I was reluctance but awhile I started noticing the beauty in this piece of work. The second person was one Afam Ekeh with Times International who was in charge of the poetry column of the Magazine that literally forced me to write something. I can remember the title of the poem, which was ‘The Moon I Point My Fingers.’ I must confess that it was not a serious work ooo. Although he published it. I can guess that it was not for its literary merit, but to motivate me to write. I will always remain grateful to him for this literary and motivational gesture. Ironically both left for USA before they could finish their self-chosen work on me. We did not finish the semester when Dr Onukaogu left for USA and same applied to Afam who left while I was doing my industrial attachment with Daily Times. When did you start writing and how many published works to your credit including fiction or non-fictional? I will say that I started writing poems more seriously in 1988. I had a poem in ANA Review then with Uche Nduka, whom I believe was the editor. It was the same time that I joined ANA Lagos and Committee for Advancement of New Authors (CANA) promoted by the trio of Chinweizu, Nwosu and the another guy that wrote the book ‘Sex Is A Nigger’s Game.’ I couldn’t remember his name. It was in his house in Apapa that we usually meet. But for ANA Lagos we used different locations like the National Museum and finally ending up in Dr Ajayi’s home the medical doctor novelist. Related News How N9,600 computer course changed my career — Designer, Chizaram The Lie I Bought: Why one Nigerian writer wants us to question ourselves ‘My chairman sir’: How begging, extortion have become new normal at airports It was during this period that we had this anthology Twenty Nigerian Writers edited by Dr Ajayi and this guy from the Mass Communication department of the University of Lagos. For the published works I will say that my works have appeared in may journals and anthologies both nationally and internationally published. I can also say that I have five serious works which are Songs of A Stranger At The Smiling Coast by Kraft Books Limited, that I would say is the most successful among them. Others are My Gambian and Other Poems by Libretto Publishers, Calligramme by Emotion Books, I Want To Paint With Words by Stripes Press, and A Love That Faded Away With Distant Cries, recently released by Kraft Books. I also have a pretty collection published by a Zimbabwean Publisher ‘Like A Starry Night.’ For the fiction, I just completed a collection of short stories titled: One Penny Ring and Other Stories. Yes there have been two collections of essays on Amazon and they are ‘Truth Beauty’ which is the motto of the secondary school that I attended that I later found to be taken from the poem of John Keats. In all I can say that my literary feet is work in progress. How do you classify your poetic style: romance, dirge or socio-politically motivated. What language do you employ most to drive your messages? I tries to be Afrocentric in my writing in the first place. I also believe that African writings have a major place in world literature. This is why I do not feel that an African writer should worry himself much about his foreign readers. I may be wrong on this position. But this is how I feel. I will want to refer myself as a generalist if there is anything like it in literature. Nevertheless, I can claim that my works are lyrical. I don’t believe that poems should be a puzzle for the readers. This is why I love African poetry. Just like songs. You understand the ‘egwu owa’ the igbo moonlight folksong stuff. I may agree that at times many poems may be socio-politically influenced. Especially those that deal with issues like hunger. I would like to make a reference from ‘SIM Now,’ a South African publication that did a little review on my writings. And I quote, “When we begin to reflect upon hunger, I draw upon the words of provocative Nigerian poet Obinna Chilekezi, who, filled with his own descriptions and impression, started writing poems at an early age. Chilekezi personalizes hunger. ‘Hunger befriends the land / The land befriends hunger,’ he writes in ‘Food comes first.’ In ‘Not just this change,’ he writes, ‘Hunger has swallowed our land whole.’ I find it compelling how Chilekezi uses an experience like hunger, which involves want and emptiness, to personify a glutton with a ravishing appetite. I also find his metaphor rather unsettling. I think this speaks much of my writings, especially my poems. My English teacher in the secondary school at Ife Secondary School, the late Mr Dominic Nwachukwu (Nnanyi Dom) would say then, “it is an Axiom, yes self-evident truth !” What messages do you drive in your poems with emphasis on societal values? I had once told African Research Forum that I am a poet that believe in Art for art’s sake. First and foremost I see my poems as works of arts. There are times like every other artists, that I can use my writings to deliver a vintage message. That is it. In your multifaceted state as a writer, how do you navigate between creative to business writing. Do they clashes with your personality as author of books in different communities? This question usually comes up in all my interviews. I have tried to attempt answering it in various media that writing and insurance have a common objective of addressing societal ills. While insurance tends to provide succour to societal mishap, writing in the other hand, tends to mirror this mishaps so that the society can not only learn from them but also provide mechanism to cater for the fall outs like insurance. This way, there has been many insurance practitioners who are writers too. Some of them were renowned that included Wallace Stevens who worked for decades as an executive and vice president at the Hartford Accident and Indemnity Company in Connecticut USA while simultaneously writing modernist poetry that won him the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1955. We also had Franz Kafka who worked as an insurance officer and claims administrator for the Workmen’s Accident Insurance Institute in Prague, drafting technical legal reports and writing existential fiction by night. Also, Tom Clancy who owned and operated an independent insurance agency (O.F. Brown Agency) in the Maryland USA before breaking out as a best-selling military thriller novelist in the 1980s. There is nothing strange for one to be an insurance practitioner and be a writer same time. There is no conflict at all. Lets talk about your other career as an insurance expert. You have continued authoring books in this field. How many books have you in your kitty and what are they focusing on? Yes, I have written many technical books on insurance and God willing will write more. I shared the African Insurance Organisation’s Book Award in 2016 with my friend Charles Nwanze. Incidentally, I am Charles too, although I prefer not to use it. For the number of books including those that I edited I can say that there are over fifteen in number. For the career I will say that I have been around industry for more than three decades that took me to different arms of the industry. Presently I am more into teaching, research and consulting. Or if you can permit me to say, writing too. Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/Pool/CNP/Shutterstock Donald Trump Trump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland Islands Comments signal president prepared to use dispute to push UK to raise defence spending and Nato contributions Robert Tait in Washington Tue 1 Sep 2026 04.31 EDT First published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 19.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump has suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands , in a move likely to strain the “special relationship” between Washington and London. “I always review every position – that’s just one of many,” the US president told reporters in the White House, in response to a question about whether he was reviewing the US’s position over the South Atlantic islands, an archipelago whose status has long been disputed by Argentina , which claims sovereignty. Officially, the US takes a neutral position on who has rightful sovereignty over the islands, which Britain first claimed in the late 17th century and has held almost continually since 1833. In practice, it recognizes British administration over the territory, which was the subject of an Argentinian invasion and subsequent military conflict with Britain in 1982. Trump’s remarks were the clearest sign yet that the administration is prepared to use the dispute as leverage to pressure the government of the new British prime minister, Andy Burnham, to raise defence spending and contributions to Nato. A spokesperson for Burnham said on Tuesday that the UK’s position on the Falkands was “crystal clear”. “The Falkland islanders are British with a right to determine their own future. The islanders have expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory, and our commitment to them is unwavering,” he said. “The prime minister was clear on his first day in office that we’ll meet our international commitments to our allies on defence spending, and he hasn’t wavered from that.” Trump’s comments came after an unnamed US official told the Telegraph last week that Washington could change its position over the islands if Britain failed to meet its defence spending commitments. That followed reports that John Healey, the UK chancellor, was preparing to drop Britain’s prior commitment to devote 3% of its GDP to defence spending by 2030 when he delivers his first budget on 28 October. Trump has made a priority of pressuring the US’s allies into boosting defence budgets and raising their Nato contributions during both his presidencies, accusing other countries of “freeloading”. At a summit in The Hague last year, allies committed to spending 5% of GDP on defence and security-related expenditures by 2035. Speculation about a US switch of allegiance over the islands has been swirling for months. In April, a leaked Pentagon email suggested reviewing Britain’s claim in response to its lack of support for Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. A switch of US position would represent a psychological blow to Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands. After Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, the decision by Margaret Thatcher’s government to dispatch a naval taskforce that eventually resulted in their recovery was bolstered by staunch diplomatic support from Ronald Reagan, who came down on Britain’s side, even though Washington was also an ally of the Argentinian ruling military junta. A total of 649 Argentinian and 255 British personnel died in fighting before Argentina’s forces surrendered in June 1982. The episode played a central role in cementing the bond between Thatcher and Reagan, who were political allies and ideological kindred spirits. In recent times, Trump has become close to Argentina’s populist president, Javier Milei, who attended his second inauguration in January last year. Last year, Trump authorized a $20bn financial lifeline to Argentina to help it navigate a financial crisis, but made the funds contingent on Milei’s party winning subsequent congressional elections. Milei’s La Libertad Avanza party duly won the election, confounding pollsters’ forecasts. Trump later authorized the importation of Argentinian beef in an effort to reduce US grocery prices. Milei has vocally supported Argentina’s claim to the islands. In a 2013 poll, 1,513 out of 1,517 Falklands residents who cast a ballot said they wanted the territory remain a part of the UK. Feelings over the islands surfaced after Argentina’s 2-1 victory over England in the semi-final of the World Cup in July, when celebrating Argentinian players unfurled a banner reading “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” – the Falklands are Argentinian. The Argentinian football association was subsequently fined $235,000 by Fifa for violating its rules on non-sporting demonstrations. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/26/saud.text: A Saudi-led coalition said on Saturday that it had intercepted drones and missiles launched by the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels towards Saudi Arabia.Turki Al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the Coalition Force, said early Saturday that they were "monitoring and tracking missile and drone threats directed at the Kingdom."He later announced that air defences had shot down two drones launched by Yemen's Houthis towards the Riyadh area as well as two ballistic missiles targeting the city of Khamis Mushait in southwestern Saudi Arabia.The Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in July and have since been launching increasing attacks on Saudi cities and shipping, further heightening tensions in the Middle East.Saudi Arabia has hit back with its own strikes on the group but has failed to stop it from seizing large stretches of territory in Yemen this month.On Friday, the Houthis said Saudi warplanes had launched 14 airstrikes and missile attacks over the previous 24 hours against the areas of Taiz, Amran, Marib, and Saada in Yemen.According to the United Nations, more than 122,000 people have been displaced by the escalation of conflict across Yemen. Between 6 August and 18 September, 674 people died and 2,998 were injured amid the conflict, the organisation reported earlier this week.

Romanian Business News - ACTMedia :: Services | About us | Contact | RSS Home Daily Financial & banking Economic Companies Energy & Environment KelemenHunor:Ilie Bolojan could remain prime minister for long time without being able to do anything Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan could remain in an acting capacity for a long time to come, says the Democratic Union of Hungarians in Romania (UDMR) President Kelemen Hunor, who also maintains that the option of early elections "must be seriously considered." "Indeed, if a government were to fall, we would certainly be heading towards early elections. This option of early elections must be considered very, very seriously. However, I have not discussed this with the President?at least when I spoke with him, we did not discuss the possibility of early elections. (...) But yes, it must be taken into account; if a government falls, then those two conditions have been met," stated Kelemen Hunor at Parliament. He added that if President Nicusor Dan nominates a prime minister who fails to secure the 233 votes needed for parliamentary investiture, the head of state has two options. "You will understand why I tried to convince my colleagues, Mr. Grindeanu and Mr. Bolojan, that we should go ahead and vote to invest even a single-party PSD government; because if we don't do this, then Mr. Bolojan remains a prime minister who has resigned or been dismissed?heading a dismissed government without full powers?and he cannot accomplish anything. If the President makes a nomination and the designated prime minister fails to secure the 233 votes, there are two possibilities: he returns the mandate, and we continue with Mr. Bolojan at the helm of the government?acting, resigned, or dismissed. If a government falls, it means Mr. Bolojan remains acting prime minister, a role he does not wish to hold. And if we end up with early elections, he would remain in government until then, unable to take the actions the whole country expects. So, no matter how we try to resolve this crisis, if we fail to invest a government, Mr. Bolojan could remain there as acting prime minister for a very long time," explained the UDMR leader. When asked if Ilie Bolojan's resignation would help at this moment?a scenario recently floated?Kelemen Hunor dismissed the idea as "foolish": "No, that is foolish. No. I don't know who floated it, or why. They even denied it yesterday. (...) If you are under the impression that President Dan can be pressured or swayed by such information from anonymous sources, I don't think he can be swayed. (...) Unfortunately, things are getting more complicated by the day. That is why we said, and repeat: 'Come on, let's put egos aside?on both sides?and invest a Government. After that, one can go into opposition; that's no problem?the very next day you're in opposition. But without voting in a Government, we just get even more tangled up.'" In his view, "the question is whether the PSD and PNL manage to reach an agreement on an investiture vote." https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2026/09.text: Menu Search Latest Profile English Contact | About | International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Menu Search International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Latest Profile Fourth International Socialist Equality Party IYSSE About the WSWS Contact Donate On September 23, New Zealand’s opposition Labour Party presented a foreign policy approach described as “independent, principled and unafraid.” New Zealand Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins [AP Photo/Robert Kitchin] The speeches by leader Chris Hipkins and foreign affairs spokesperson Vanushi Walters had an air of unreality. They largely consisted of bland phrases about the need for more “diplomacy” and “the peaceful resolution of conflicts and disputes.” On the same day, US President Donald Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that he was deciding whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” of Iran and “drive them into hell with no chance of survival.” Hipkins and Walters did not mention, let alone condemn, Trump’s genocidal threats and the criminal war against Iran, part of an expanding global war in which New Zealand’s ruling class is complicit as an ally of US imperialism. With an election looming on November 7, Labour is highly conscious of anti-war sentiment. The war against Iran, which has led to soaring prices, is opposed by nearly nine in ten people in New Zealand. Protests continue against the US-Israeli genocide in Gaza, and the US is viewed as a greater threat than China, according to one survey. Labour is attempting to rhetorically distance itself from Washington, while remaining fully committed to the military-intelligence alliance with US imperialism. The 2017–2023 Labour-Greens government supported the military build-up against China in the Indo-Pacific region and the US-NATO war against Russia over Ukraine. The media highlighted Walters’ statement that a Labour-led government would recognise the state of Palestine, impose “economic sanctions on Israel,” and support South Africa’s case in the International Court of Justice arguing that Israel has breached the Genocide Convention. Walters criticised the National Party-led government for its “silence” on the genocide and for “failing to stand up a sanctions regime.” This had damaged NZ’s reputation as an “honest broker,” she said. Labour’s own record on Gaza is one of active complicity followed by belated, disingenuous crocodile tears. Following October 7, 2023, the Labour government joined the US and every other imperialist power in declaring support for Israel’s “right to defend itself” against “terrorism”—the fraudulent pretext for the slaughter of Palestinians. This stance contributed to Labour’s crushing defeat in the October 14 election. On November 7, 2023, Hipkins (who was still the caretaker prime minister) again refused to condemn Israel, which had by then killed more than 11,000 people, saying he was “not going to make a judgement” about whether it had breached international law. Labour MPs were booed when they tried to speak to protesters and posture as supporters of the Palestinian people. Three years later, with Gaza in ruins, Labour’s proposed sanctions are entirely hypocritical. Hipkins made clear that a Labour-led government will strengthen NZ’s alliance with the United States, a full partner in the ongoing genocide of the Palestinians and the widening war against Lebanon and Iran. Hipkins said it was “vital” that New Zealand remain in the Five Eyes, the intelligence sharing network led by the US, which also includes Australia, Canada and the UK. Seeking to downplay the Five Eyes, he said it was “not a formal military alliance.” The Five Eyes partners, however, are actively spying on China, the Middle East and elsewhere and discussing war plans against China. At a public meeting on September 19, Hipkins similarly defended the government’s decision to allow the FBI to open a permanent office in Wellington. He declared: “this might sound unusual coming from a lefty politician like me, but it’s actually quite helpful to us,” claiming it provided important information from “like-minded countries.” Opening the office last year, FBI director Kash Patel said its purpose was “countering the CCP [Chinese Communist Party]” in the Indo-Pacific “theatre”—i.e. preparing for war. Hipkins said on September 23 that the US and China were both among New Zealand’s “most important partners,” adding: “I reject the idea that countries like New Zealand must choose between one relationship and another.” Walters criticised current Foreign Minister Winston Peters, from the far-right NZ First Party, for his “outright racism” towards Chinese people. Successive governments have, in fact, firmly aligned New Zealand with US warmongering. The 2017–2023 Labour-led government, which included the Greens, repeatedly issued statements denouncing China and Russia as the main “threats” facing the world. In August 2023, then Defence Minister Andrew Little stated that NZ needed “a combat capable, ready force,” adding: “If for example conflict does break out in the South China Sea, where $20 billion of our exports flows through every year, we have a stake in that, and we may be called on to play a role.” Hipkins declared last week that Labour would not join the AUKUS agreement between the US, Australia and Britain, under which Australia is being further militarised and will be armed with nuclear-powered attack submarines. Ask more questions at SocialismAI.com He added, however, that “we will work with partners on the new frontiers of security, including artificial intelligence in weaponry and the militarisation of space.” The Labour leader described NZ’s alliance with Australia as one of “the closest relationships any two countries share.” Australia has been transformed into a vast base for military operations against China; the US controls or has access to more than 110 defence facilities there. The New Zealand military’s extremely close integration with Australia’s armed forces means that it is automatically part of these war preparations. Australia and New Zealand are both imperialist powers and have dominated much of the Pacific region for more than a century. They have always relied on the support of the major imperialist power—first Britain and then, after World War II, the US. Labour governments have actively supported criminal imperialist wars led by the US, including by sending New Zealand troops to Afghanistan in 2001 and Iraq in 2003. As well as joining the military build-up against China, the last Labour-led government actively supported the US-NATO proxy war against Russia by sending NZ troops to Britain to train Ukrainian conscripts. The current government has also deployed troops to Poland. Hipkins declared that Labour would “continue to support Ukraine in defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity.” This is a fraud. In the name of “independence” and “freedom,” Ukraine’s far-right regime has turned the country into a police state and placed it at the disposal of the US and NATO. Having provoked Russia’s disastrous invasion in 2022, the imperialist powers are escalating the war, sacrificing hundreds of thousands of lives, so that they can plunder the resources of Ukraine and of Russia itself. Left-wing and anti-war parties are banned within Ukraine and a court has sentenced the socialist Bogdan Syrotiuk to 15 years in prison for the “crime” of calling on Russian and Ukrainian workers to unite and put an end to the war. The working class must be warned: another Labour government will continue and escalate New Zealand’s involvement in the widening world war. It will rapidly increase military spending and recruitment , which will be funded by cutting social programs and workers’ living standards. The Greens and the union bureaucracy will work with Labour to enforce this agenda. To stop the plunge into world war and barbarism, workers and young people must break from all the capitalist parties and build a new movement, based on the program of socialist internationalism, to put an end to the capitalist system which is the source of war.
